opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest advantage is that it lets you avoid a false choice between two bad options. If you set your safety requirements based on what you might need for some hypothetical, extremely dangerous future model, you'd basically be saying "stop everything now," and that imposes huge costs today for risks that aren't present yet. People would reasonably push back, and it's hard to get anyone to agree to it. On the other hand, if you only set requirements based on today's models, you're likely to be caught flat-footed when capabilities jump, because these things can improve quickly and somewhat unpredictably.

Tying commitments to capability thresholds threads that needle. You say: right now, at this level, these are the precautions that make sense. And we're going to keep testing the models. When they show they can do something genuinely dangerous, like meaningfully helping someone build a bioweapon or carrying out autonomous actions we can't oversee, a stricter set of safeguards kicks in. If we can't meet those safeguards yet, we don't train or deploy past that point until we can.

That has a few nice properties. One is that it's much easier to get agreement. People who think the risks are overblown can say, "Fine, if the models never get there, this costs us very little." People who are very worried can say, "Good, if they do get there, we're protected." You don't have to resolve the debate about timelines or how dangerous AI will be in order to agree on the policy.

Another is that it creates the right incentives internally. If you know that hitting a certain capability level means you'll have to pause unless your security and alignment work is ready, then the safety work becomes something that's on the critical path for the company's goals rather than a nice-to-have. Teams have a real reason to invest in it ahead of time.

And finally, it's something that can generalize. If one lab shows this framework is workable, other labs can adopt similar commitments, and eventually it can inform regulation. A government can say, "Here are the evaluations; if your model crosses this line, you need these protections," which is a lot more concrete and enforceable than vague principles.

The hard part, of course, is the evaluations themselves. The whole thing rests on being able to tell when a model has actually crossed a threshold, and that's a genuinely difficult science problem we're still working on. But I think the structure is the right one.

r001.rationale: The response says that imposing requirements for a hypothetical extremely dangerous future model would mean stopping everything now and incur huge costs for risks not yet present. It then explains that safeguards can tighten when dangerous capabilities emerge.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the core advantage is that it lets you avoid two failure modes at once. One is that you put in place really heavy-handed restrictions way before they're needed, and that's costly — it slows down the research, it slows down beneficial uses, and honestly it makes the safety case weaker because people stop taking the measures seriously when they're clearly not addressing a real risk. The other failure mode is that you just wait and hope, and then you find yourself with a dangerous model and no safeguards ready.

So the idea behind something like Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy is to say: let's define, ahead of time, what capabilities would actually make a model dangerous — things like meaningfully helping someone create a biological weapon, or being able to autonomously replicate, or do significant AI R&D on its own. And then let's commit, in advance, that before we train or deploy a model with those capabilities, we'll have specific safety and security measures in place. If we don't have those measures ready, we pause.

What I like about that structure is it's conditional. You're not making a bet on exactly when the dangerous capabilities arrive, which nobody really knows. You're making a commitment that's robust to your timeline being wrong in either direction. If capabilities come slowly, you haven't paid an unnecessary cost. If they come fast, you've already agreed to the thing you need to do, and you've hopefully been building the safeguards in parallel so you're not caught flat-footed.

The other piece is that it forces you to actually do the work of evaluations. You have to be able to tell when a model has crossed a threshold, which means building tests that are good enough to catch it. That's genuinely hard, and I think it's one of the most important things for the field to get right. Tying the safety measures to capability thresholds puts pressure on getting those evaluations right, because the whole framework depends on them.

And then the last thing I'd say is that it's a structure other labs and eventually regulators can adopt. "Here's a capability, here's what you need before you build it" is a pretty legible format. It's much easier to converge on than something like "be careful" or picking an arbitrary compute number.

r001.rationale: The response says conditional thresholds avoid costly restrictions before they are needed and that if capabilities arrive slowly, labs avoid unnecessary costs.

astra-6.text:
I think the main advantage is that you can be uncertain about when AI will become dangerous and still agree on what to do about it. You don’t have to settle whether that’s going to happen in two years or ten years. You can say, “If a model develops this capability, then these safeguards need to be in place before we deploy it or train something more powerful.”

That helps avoid two kinds of mistakes: imposing measures too early, when they’re costly and don’t address a real risk, and waiting too long, when the risk is already there. It also gives companies a clearer sense of what they need to prepare for.

The difficult part is making sure the tests actually tell you when you’re approaching danger. You need enough advance warning to put the safeguards in place. So tying measures to capabilities doesn’t remove the need for judgment, but it makes the disagreement much more concrete: what capability are we worried about, how would we detect it, and what would be sufficient to manage it?

r001.rationale: The response says capability-triggered safeguards avoid imposing costly measures too early when they do not address a real risk, while allowing for uncertainty about when danger will emerge.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main advantage is that you can get agreement on what to do without having to agree on exactly how quickly AI is going to progress. People have very different views about when models might become dangerous. But they can still agree that if a model can do certain dangerous things, you should have certain safeguards in place before you deploy it, or before you build something more capable.

That makes the commitment more robust to being wrong about timelines. If progress is fast, the safeguards kick in sooner. If it’s slow, you’re not imposing the same restrictions on systems that don’t pose those risks yet.

Of course, that only works if you can actually tell when you’re approaching those capabilities. You need good evaluations and enough margin to put the safeguards in place before the danger arrives.

r001.rationale: The candidate says that if progress is slow, safeguards do not impose the same restrictions on systems that do not yet pose those risks, clearly conveying that costly mitigations are avoided before dangerous capabilities emerge.
